q: The earliest expression of the computational view of thought, per Haugeland, is Hobbes':
e: It took three centuries, until electronic computers, for the idea to catch on.

q: For Haugeland, what makes a project count as AI isn't protoplasm vs. semiconductor, but whether:
a: It's designed in terms of a computational structure
w: It's built by a large computer company like IBM
It runs on electricity rather than chemistry
It can pass the Turing Test in conversation
e: The product is designed and specified in terms of a computational structure. A DuPont synthetic-organic android probably wouldn't count. An IBM programmed robot probably would.

q: Which three dilemmas does Haugeland say the computational idea 'slices through at a stroke'?
w: Free will, God, and personal immortality
Qualia, zombies, and the inverted spectrum
e: Mind/matter interaction, explaining meaning without a homunculus, and the testability of mentalistic explanation. Cognitive scientists can be materialists AND mentalists, explaining by rules without an unexplained homunculus.

q: Why does Haugeland say there can't be a dynamics of thought like physical dynamics?
a: Following reason's rules seems to need a rule-applier
w: Thoughts are far too small to measure physically
Thoughts happen randomly, with no laws at all
The laws of physics don't apply inside brains
e: Particles obey laws infallibly, but people must work to follow rules of reason, which seems to require an understanding rule-applier. That rule-applier looks like a homunculus 'directing thoughts like a traffic cop', which begs the question.

q: Haugeland says the chess-playing machine is philosophically inspiring because:
a: It reasons physically without needing a homunculus
w: It always wins its games against human grandmasters
It is fully conscious of every move it decides to make
It has an immaterial soul that guides its choices
e: Its decisions cause physical behavior without violating physics or needing an unexplained 'compunculus'. It follows rules of the game and rules of thumb, and there's a determinate answer about what reasoning it went through.

q: Haugeland defines a computer as:
e: A formal system is like a game where tokens are manipulated according to rules.

q: To define a formal system you specify three things:
a: The tokens, the starting position, and the legal moves
w: Inputs, outputs, and the internal states between them
Syntax, semantics, and pragmatics of the symbols
Hardware, software, and the users of the system
e: What the tokens are, the starting position, and what moves are allowed. Example: peg-jumping solitaire, where the goal is one peg left in the center.

q: A formal system is 'digital' because it is:
w: Electronic, very fast, and based on binary
Analog, continuous, and approximate in value
e: The weather or the state of the economy make no difference to the game. There are no borderline cases.

q: The domino triad-switching game turns out to be 'essentially the same' as peg-jumping. This illustrates:
e: Positions correspond one-to-one, starting positions correspond, and legal moves correspond.

q: In fancy chess sets, every pawn figurine is different, but they're all the same TYPE because:
w: They're made of the same material
They start on the same row of the board
e: The rules treat them identically: tokens of the same type are formally interchangeable. Type is fixed by how the rules treat a token, not by its appearance.

q: How can the algebra game have finitely checkable moves despite indefinitely many formula types?
a: Formulas are built from a few atomic tokens
w: Only a small number of formulas are allowed
Moves in the algebra game are never checked
Algebra isn't really a formal system at all
e: Formulas are built from a small set of atomic tokens, and rules apply by structure. Positions of one system (the well-formed-formula game) serve as tokens of a higher-level system.

q: Combining Church's thesis and Turing's theorem gives the result that a universal Turing machine can:
w: Eventually become conscious if it runs long enough
Run any program without needing any memory
e: Imitate any automatic formal system whatsoever (given programming). Real computers are universal machines, except that their storage is limited.

q: When a Turing machine imitates another system, the part that corresponds directly to the imitated system is the ______, and the behind-the-scenes part is the ______.
e: Languages like BASIC, FORTRAN, LISP are really convenient universal machines imitated by hardware.

q: Why does Haugeland say it's foolish to call computers 'nothing but number crunchers'?
a: One object can be many machines at different levels
w: Computers don't actually use numbers internally
Computers are conscious of what they compute
Numbers aren't real, so nothing crunches them
e: A physical object can be many machines at once, and the level that matters may have nothing to do with bits. A particular object is a particular machine only at a particular level of description.

q: The 'control problem' in automating a formal system is:
a: Choosing which legal move to make
w: Getting the device to obey the rules
e: How the device selects which move to make when several are legal. In chess, listing legal moves is easy. Choosing among them is the difference between amateurs and world champions.

q: Looking ahead 40 moves in chess would involve about 10¹²⁰ possibilities. This is called:
e: Fewer than 10¹⁸ seconds have passed since the universe began. The solution is to consider only relevant moves.

q: An algorithm is guaranteed to give a result meeting certain conditions. A heuristic is:
a: A useful rule of thumb that can fail
w: A rule that is guaranteed to always fail
A random guess made when stuck
A hardware component in the machine
e: A more-or-less reliable rule of thumb that isn't infallible. 'Never trade your queen for a pawn' is a heuristic for winning. A machine can infallibly follow fallible rules.

q: A multi-position selector switch vs. a continuous tuning dial illustrates:
e: You can't set a switch between AM and FM, but a dial can sit between stations.

q: What's the 'overwhelming advantage' of poker chips over tablespoons of colored sand?
w: Chips are far cheaper to produce
Chips are more colorful and easy to see
e: All bets are exact: digital tokens eliminate measurement error that propagates. With ±2% sand error, betting 613 is pointless (the white units drop out). With chips, 613 is easy.

q: Why does Haugeland call 'any analog device can be digitally simulated' grossly misleading?
a: Simulation needs a precise description many systems lack
w: Digital computers are always too slow to keep up
Analog devices don't really exist in the world
Digital simulation is always perfect in principle
e: Simulation needs a compact, precise description of the relevant relationships, which systems like drugged lab rats lack. 'In principle, rats are made of atoms' is 'utterly out to lunch'.

q: Formal tokens can lead 'two lives'. They are:
e: Syntactical (meaningless markers moved by rules) and semantic (having meanings related to the world). How the two lives get together is the foundation of modern logic and the inspiration of cognitive science.

q: Given true axioms and truth-preserving rules, 'if you take care of the syntax, ______.'
a: The semantics will take care of itself
w: The hardware will take care of itself
The homunculus will take care of it
e: So proving a theorem formally establishes its semantic truth.

q: An automatic formal system with an interpretation such that the semantics takes care of itself is what Dennett calls a:
e: The discovery that semantic engines are possible is the basic inspiration of cognitive science and AI.

q: The 'arithmetic salad' example shows that, among trillions of interpretations of the same tokens, we prefer the one that:
a: Makes the outputs come out true
w: Is the simplest one to write down
Makes the outputs look like equations
e: Makes the outputs come out true (and sensible). The tokens themselves never favor one interpretation. Truth is what makes one 'righter'.

q: 'GOFAI' stands for:
e: Also called classical, symbol-manipulation, or language-of-thought AI. It dominated from the mid-50s through the mid-80s.

q: Symbols differ from chess pieces in that:
a: Symbols mean something; chess pieces don't
w: Symbols are physical, but chess pieces aren't
Chess pieces are digital, but symbols aren't
There is no real difference between the two
e: Symbols mean something; chess pieces are merely formal game tokens. Numerals represent numbers. Chess pieces, checkers and go stones represent nothing.

q: Haugeland says all interpretation, including translation, is:
e: Holistic: you can't interpret a brief string completely out of context. A single string might come out true on two schemes by coincidence. Only a consistent pattern across many cases matters.

q: For a system's intermediate token strings to count as genuine reasoning steps, it must:
a: Solve an open range of problems through those steps
w: Be built from biological neurons, like a brain
Be conscious of each step as it happens
Solve every problem instantly without searching
e: Handle an open-ended range of problems AND actually arrive at solutions through those steps. Otherwise it's 'a kind of fraud', e.g., solving another way and tacking on fake 'steps'.

q: Early GOFAI systems were clever on carefully posed problems but prone to amusing blunders because they lacked:
e: Later work shifted to large-scale knowledge representation, where the biggest problem was organization.

q: Which is NOT one of the disappointments of GOFAI Haugeland lists?
e: Explicit reasoning is GOFAI's strength. Its weaknesses led some to explore 'new-fangled AI' (NFAI).

q: Connectionist networks differ from GOFAI in having:
a: Many simple units, no central processor
w: Explicit symbolic rules for every task
e: Many simple interconnected units with no central processor and no separate memory store. Connectionism is the most prominent 'NFAI' approach. It addresses GOFAI's weaknesses but isn't yet good at its strengths.
